quick q while i get coffee: whats actually different between structuredClone(x) and JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))

```js
const a = { d: new Date(), m: new Map([[1, 'x']]), u: undefined };
structuredClone(a);              // Date stays a Date, Map stays a Map, u kept
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(a));   // d becomes a string, m becomes {}, u dropped
```

structuredClone uses the same algorithm browsers use to copy data between windows and workers. It keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays, and handles circular references. The JSON round trip only keeps plain JSON values: Dates turn into strings, Maps and Sets become empty objects, undefined and functions disappear, and a circular reference throws. Neither one copies functions or class prototypes (a class instance comes back as a plain object), and structuredClone throws on functions instead of silently dropping them.

events.text:
How it works today: on SIGTERM the worker stops taking new jobs and drains the in-flight ones, with a 30 second grace period (`GRACE_PERIOD_MS = 30_000` in services/worker/src/shutdown.ts). After 30 seconds it exits with code 1 and BullMQ marks the abandoned jobs as stalled. The Helm chart also sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`, so Kubernetes would SIGKILL at the same moment anyway.

The previous pod's logs show the real problem. An image-resize job *started* about a second after SIGTERM, and the pod hit the 30s limit while it was still running. Two things are on our side: `w.close()` lets the worker pick up one more job while it's closing, and image jobs can take longer than 30s. Possible fixes are pausing the workers before close and raising both grace values together (for example 90s in the app and 100s in Helm). I haven't changed anything yet.

events.text: unrelated, trailmix question. django orm: how do i annotate each Hike with its photo count and only keep hikes with more than 3 photos

```python
from django.db.models import Count

hikes = (
    Hike.objects
    .annotate(photo_count=Count("photos", distinct=True))
    .filter(photo_count__gt=3)
    .order_by("-photo_count")
)
```

`"photos"` is the related name of the Photo foreign key to Hike (use `photo` if you didn't set a related_name). Filtering on an annotation after `.annotate()` becomes a `HAVING` clause in SQL. Keep `distinct=True` if you also annotate across another relation like tags in the same query; otherwise the joins multiply the counts. For HTMX partials, `hike.photo_count` is then available directly in the template.

events.text: random q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled, when does the difference actually bite

```ts
await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()]);        // rejects as soon as one rejects
await Promise.allSettled([a(), b(), c()]); // always resolves: [{status, value|reason}, ...]
```

`Promise.all` rejects with the first error, and you lose the results of the others even though they keep running in the background. That bites when the tasks are independent, like sending ten emails: one failure throws away the information about which nine succeeded. `allSettled` waits for everything and tells you each outcome, so you can retry only the failures. Use `all` when the results only make sense together (load user + org + permissions for one page). Use `allSettled` for fan-out work where partial success is fine.

events.text: how does http/2 multiplexing actually differ from http/1.1 keep-alive? someone in standup said they're the same thing

They're not the same. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses one TCP connection for several requests, but one at a time: request 2 can't start until response 1 has fully arrived (pipelining existed but was broken in practice). That's why browsers open about 6 connections per host. HTTP/2 multiplexing splits every request and response into small frames tagged with a stream id and interleaves them on a single connection, so dozens of requests are in flight at once and a slow response doesn't block the others at the HTTP level. The remaining catch is TCP itself: one lost packet still stalls every stream on that connection. That head-of-line blocking is what HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes.

events.text: whats tsx actually doing differently from ts-node under the hood

tsx compiles each file with esbuild and only strips the types; it doesn't type-check. That's why it starts almost instantly and handles ESM, CommonJS and tsconfig paths with no setup. ts-node uses the real TypeScript compiler by default, so it type-checks as it goes (slower to start, but it catches type errors at run time), and its ESM support needs a loader flag and has historically been fiddly. In practice: tsx for running scripts and dev servers, and keep `tsc --noEmit` in CI for the actual type checking.

is there any real perf difference between Map and a plain object for string keys

Yes, for dynamic keys. A Map is built for frequent adds and deletes and doesn't degrade; objects with many changing keys fall out of V8's fast "shape" mode into slower dictionary mode, and `delete` is especially costly. For a fixed set of keys known up front (config, records), objects are as fast or faster and serialize to JSON for free. Map also keeps insertion order for all keys, has `.size`, and can't collide with prototype keys like `__proto__`.

and WeakMap. when would i actually reach for one

When you want to attach data to an object you don't own, without keeping that object alive. Examples: caching a computed value per DOM node or per request object, or storing private per-instance state for a class. Once the key object is garbage collected, the entry goes with it, so there's no leak and no cleanup code. Keys must be objects, and you can't iterate or get a size, so it only fits the "look it up by this object" case.

events.text: explain container queries vs media queries quick

Media queries look at the viewport: "if the screen is under 640px, do X". Container queries look at the size of a parent element: "if *this card's container* is under 400px, do X". That makes a component respond to the space it actually has, so the same chart works in a narrow sidebar on a wide screen. In Tailwind v4 you mark the parent with `@container` and use variants like `@sm:` or `@md:` on the children.
